title: Macroscale Gradients and Intrinsic Neural Timescales

html:
Across cortex-and mirrored in several subcortical systems-organization is better captured by smooth gradients than by sharp borders. The dominant cortical axis ("principal gradient") runs from unimodal sensorimotor areas to transmodal association cortex (default-mode and frontoparietal zones). Along this path, myeloarchitecture thins, pyramidal dendrites lengthen, receptive fields broaden, and connectivity shifts from short-range, topographically precise links to long-range, integrative projections. Functionally, this same axis separates fast, stimulus-locked processing from slow, model-based inference. Diffusion-map embeddings of resting connectivity first made this explicit, placing primary visual/auditory/somatomotor cortex at one end and default-mode cortex at the other, with higher association zones in between. T1w/T2w myelin maps and multimodal parcellations recapitulate the same sensorimotor->association gradient, tying the functional axis to a structural substrate 1, 2, 3.

Temporal organization follows this geometry. Electrophysiology across primate cortex shows a monotonic increase in intrinsic timescales-from tens of milliseconds in early sensory areas to hundreds of milliseconds or more in prefrontal and midline association cortices-consistent with a hierarchy that integrates over progressively longer windows as one ascends the gradient. Naturalistic fMRI pushes this further: "temporal receptive windows" expand from word/phoneme-scale in early auditory cortex to sentence/paragraph-scale in superior temporal, angular gyrus, and medial prefrontal cortex, supporting narrative-level inference and event segmentation. Together these data argue that the cortex is wired to accumulate evidence over time in proportion to its position on the sensorimotor->association gradient: posterior/lateral regions compress immediate input; anterior/medial regions stabilize context over seconds to minutes 4, 5, 6.

Hippocampus exhibits a homologous long-axis gradient. Posterior hippocampus couples to posterior-medial, perceptual networks and emphasizes precise spatial/contextual coding and pattern separation; anterior hippocampus couples to anterior-temporal/ventromedial networks and emphasizes coarse, affect- and schema-laden representations and pattern completion. This posterior->anterior sweep aligns with a short->long horizon in mnemonic integration and abstraction, positioning hippocampus as a bridge between fast sensory maps and slow, schema-driven simulation 7, 8.

Comparable gradients appear outside neocortex. In cerebellum, a principal functional gradient runs from sensorimotor lobules to DMN- and control-network-coupled territories, with a secondary axis differentiating task-focused from task-unfocused cognition; this mirrors the neocortical principal gradient and suggests that cerebellar forward models operate over short horizons in motor zones and longer, more abstract sequences in cognitive zones. Thalamus, too, shows low-dimensional gradients that align with cortical hierarchies, offering a substrate for routing information across timescales via core (driver) and matrix (modulatory) channels. These parallel gradients imply that hierarchical timescales are not a cortical curiosity but a whole-brain design principle implemented across loops 9, 10.

Mechanistically, gradients and timescales co-vary with three families of constraints. First, cyto/myeloarchitectonics: lightly myelinated, homotypical (eulaminate) association cortex with long apical dendrites (DMN, anterior PFC) supports slower membrane and network dynamics and stronger feedback, lengthening integration windows; heavily myelinated heterotypical granular cortex (V1/A1/S1) favors fast feedforward drive and short windows. Second, wiring geometry: as geodesic distance from primary landmarks increases, long-range associative tracts and hub participation rise, boosting recurrent mixing and temporal stability. Third, neuromodulatory/thalamic tone: association cortex receives denser higher-order (matrix-type) thalamic input and neuromodulatory afferents that tune gain and plasticity over seconds-to-minutes, effectively stretching the ’temporal kernel’ of inference. The resulting system implements hierarchical inference in time: lower tiers encode rapidly changing causes; mid-tiers integrate over episodes; top tiers carry slowly drifting latent states, goals, and schemas that regularize lower levels via feedback." 2, 11, 12, 13.
